planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery-grown container stock in fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil along a streambank, seep, or shaded slope.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery-grown container stock in fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil along a streambank, seep, or shaded slope, mimicking the subalpine forest openings and avalanche chutes of the Cascades and northern Rockies where it grows wild. Unlike most rhododendrons, its cream-white flowers open along the stem below the newest leaves rather than in a terminal truss, giving it a distinctive, informal look in a woodland or native shrub border. It struggles in hot, humid summers and is best reserved for cool-climate gardens with reliable moisture and good air movement.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant container-grown nursery stock in spring into moist, strongly acidic, sandy peat along the edges of pocosins or seepage bogs in partial shade; source only nursery-propagated plants since this is a globally rare species.

directions: Plant container-grown nursery stock in spring into moist, strongly acidic, sandy peat along the edges of pocosins or seepage bogs in partial shade, replicating the fire-maintained wetland margins of the Cape Fear region of the Carolinas where this rare deciduous Kalmia is endemic. In late spring it produces small white, maroon-marked, urn-shaped flowers on bare stems just as the narrow leaves emerge, a charming and unusual look among garden Kalmia. Because it is a globally rare species of conservation concern, source only nursery-propagated plants and give it the same acidic, saturated conditions as its pocosin neighbors like sweetbay and fetterbush.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into sharply drained, humus-poor, acidic rocky or gravelly soil in a sheltered rock garden or trough.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into sharply drained, humus-poor, acidic rocky or gravelly soil in a sheltered rock garden or trough, echoing the serpentine outcrops of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains where this Oregon endemic is found nowhere else on Earth. In spring it bears small, bright rose-pink, rhododendron-like flowers over a dense mound of tiny evergreen leaves, making it a prized miniature for alpine and rock gardens. It demands cool nights, high humidity, and drainage that never stays soggy, so raised beds or scree plantings suit it far better than ordinary garden soil.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service Species Status Assessment

planting.note: Plant small container starts in spring into acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil under light conifer shade.

directions: Plant small container starts in spring into acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil under light conifer shade, matching the high-elevation forest understory of the Rockies and Cascades where this wiry, broom-like shrub carpets the ground. Its tiny leaves and green, angled twigs give it a fine, airy texture quite different from other huckleberries, and its small pink urn flowers give way to tart red berries that are a critical late-summer food source for grouse and black bears. It spreads slowly by rhizome into low colonies and is best used as a textural groundcover in a cool woodland or native rock garden rather than for significant fruit production.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
